Project Objectives¶

The primary objectives of this project are to:

  1. Develop a comprehensive understanding of the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset.
  2. Identify key risk factors that contribute to diabetes.
  3. Build a predictive model to classify patients as diabetic or non-diabetic based on clinical features.
  4. Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and validation techniques including cross-validation and threshold tuning.
  5. Provide data-driven insights and clinical recommendations to inform healthcare decisions for diabetes screening and management.

Feature Descriptions¶

Feature Meaning
Pregnancies Number of times the woman has been pregnant.
Glucose Plasma glucose concentration measured during a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). It indicates blood sugar level. Higher values may suggest diabetes.
BloodPressure Diastolic blood pressure (the lower number in a blood pressure reading), measured in mm Hg. Example: in 120/80 mm Hg, 80 is the diastolic pressure.
SkinThickness Thickness of the triceps skin fold in millimeters (mm). It is used as an estimate of body fat percentage.
Insulin 2-hour serum insulin level measured in μU/mL (micro units per milliliter) after the glucose tolerance test. It reflects how much insulin the body produces.
BMI Body Mass Index, calculated as: BMI = weight (kg) / height (m²). It indicates whether a person is underweight, normal weight, overweight, or obese.
DiabetesPedigreeFunction A score that estimates the genetic likelihood of diabetes based on family history. Higher values indicate a stronger hereditary influence.
Age Age of the person in years. Older age is generally associated with a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

Target Variable¶

Feature Meaning
Outcome Indicates whether the person has diabetes. 0 = No diabetes, 1 = Diabetes.

Example Record¶

Pregnancies Glucose BloodPressure BMI Age Outcome
2 138 62 33.6 47 1

Interpretation¶

  • The woman had 2 pregnancies.
  • Her glucose level was 138 mg/dL.
  • Her diastolic blood pressure was 62 mm Hg.
  • Her BMI was 33.6.
  • She was 47 years old.
  • The outcome 1 indicates that she had diabetes.

Important Notes¶

Some features contain 0 values that are medically unrealistic and are often treated as missing values during preprocessing:

  • Glucose = 0
  • BloodPressure = 0
  • SkinThickness = 0
  • Insulin = 0
  • BMI = 0

These values are commonly replaced using imputation techniques such as:

  • Median imputation
  • Mean imputation
  • K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) imputation

Understanding these features helps in:

  • Performing effective Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA).
  • Choosing appropriate data preprocessing techniques.
  • Interpreting machine learning model predictions more meaningfully.

📊 Skewness Analysis of Features (Diabetes Dataset)¶

🔴 Right-Skewed Features (Positive Skew)¶

These features have a long tail on the right side, meaning most values are small with a few very large values:

  • Pregnancies → right-skewed
  • Glucose → slightly right-skewed
  • BMI → slightly right-skewed
  • DiabetesPedigreeFunction → heavily right-skewed
  • Age → heavily right-skewed
  • Insulin → heavily right-skewed

🟡 Approximately Normal / Near Symmetric¶

These features are closer to a normal distribution but not perfectly symmetric:

  • BloodPressure → approximately normal
  • SkinThickness → approximately normal (slight skew may exist)

🧠 Key Insight¶

  • Most features in this dataset are right-skewed
  • Very few features follow a normal distribution
  • This is common in real-world medical datasets

🚀 Why This Matters¶

Skewness affects machine learning preprocessing:

For right-skewed features:¶

  • Log transformation (log1p)
  • Robust scaling

For near-normal features:¶

  • StandardScaler works well

💡 Conclusion¶

The dataset contains a mix of:

  • Strongly right-skewed features (Age, Insulin, DiabetesPedigreeFunction)
  • Mildly skewed features (Glucose, BMI)
  • Near-normal features (BloodPressure, SkinThickness)

Understanding this helps in choosing the right preprocessing strategy before model training.

Target Variable Distribution¶

  • The dataset contains more healthy patients (Outcome = 0) than diabetic patients (Outcome = 1).
  • Approximately 65% of the observations belong to the healthy class, while 35% belong to the diabetic class.
  • This indicates that the dataset is moderately imbalanced.
  • Since the imbalance is not extremely severe (roughly 2:1), many machine learning algorithms can still perform well. However, evaluation metrics such as Precision, Recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC should be considered in addition to accuracy.

Feature-Target Correlation Analysis¶

Feature Correlation Strength
Glucose 0.51 Moderate-High
Insulin 0.33 Moderate
BMI 0.33 Moderate
Age 0.25 Low-Moderate
Pregnancies 0.24 Low-Moderate
SkinThickness 0.24 Low-Moderate
DiabetesPedigreeFunction 0.22 Low-Moderate
BloodPressure 0.19 Low

Correlations computed on training set only (post train/test split) to avoid data leakage.

Key Insights¶

Strong Signal¶

  • Glucose is the strongest individual predictor (0.51), which aligns with medical knowledge — high blood sugar is a defining characteristic of diabetes.

Moderate Contributors¶

  • Insulin and BMI are tied as the second strongest predictors (0.33 each). Clinically this makes sense: insulin resistance and obesity are core diabetes risk factors.

Low-Moderate Contributors¶

  • Age (0.25), Pregnancies (0.24), SkinThickness (0.24), and DiabetesPedigreeFunction (0.22) all fall in the same low-moderate range. Each has clinical grounding (age-related risk, gestational history, adiposity proxy, and genetic predisposition respectively).

Weakest Predictor¶

  • BloodPressure (0.19) is the only feature in the Low category and the only one without clear boxplot separation between classes. Still retained — it may contribute through interaction effects with other features.

Important Caveat¶

Linear correlation only captures LINEAR relationships. These features may have non-linear relationships with the target that a model like Random Forest would capture but Pearson correlation would miss.

Feature Importance Summary¶

Tier 1 - Strong Predictors¶

  • Glucose (0.51): Highest correlation + clear boxplot separation. Clinically valid — high blood sugar defines diabetes.

  • Pregnancies (0.24): Low-moderate correlation but clear median separation in boxplot. Clinically valid — gestational diabetes risk increases with more pregnancies.

  • Age (0.25): Clear median separation in boxplot. Clinically valid — older age increases Type 2 diabetes risk.

Tier 2 - Moderate Predictors¶

  • Insulin (0.33): 2nd strongest correlation (tied with BMI). After correcting for data leakage (train/test split before KNN imputation), boxplot now shows visible median separation between classes. Outlier influence still under investigation — separation may become clearer when extreme values are excluded.

  • BMI (0.33): Tied 2nd strongest correlation. Obesity is a core diabetes risk factor — important feature.

Tier 3 - Weak Individual Predictors¶

  • DiabetesPedigreeFunction (0.22): Weak linear correlation but encodes genetic history — likely has non-linear importance.

  • SkinThickness (0.24): Weak predictor individually, but shows median separation in boxplot.

  • BloodPressure (0.19): Only feature with no clear median separation in boxplot after re-imputation. Weakest visual and statistical predictor. Retained as it may contribute in combination with other features.

Key Conclusion¶

No single feature will be dropped. After re-running EDA with a proper train/test split before KNN imputation (eliminating leakage risk), most features show meaningful median separation between classes — BloodPressure being the sole exception. Even weak individual predictors may contribute through:

  1. Interaction effects with other features
  2. Non-linear relationships (captured by tree-based models like Random Forest)
  3. Combined pattern recognition in the model

after commpletion of EDA, we do pre-Processing¶

since we have found that most feature are right skewed as well as huge number out outlier, we use the method of log transformation to make the data more normal and to reduce the effect of outliers in the data.

In [27]:
def transform_features(df):
    skewed_cols  = ["Pregnancies", "Insulin", 
               "DiabetesPedigreeFunction", "Age"]
    df_transformed = df.copy()
    df_transformed[skewed_cols] = df_transformed[skewed_cols ].apply(lambda x: np.log1p(x))
    # Verify skewness reduced
    print("Before transformation:")
    print(df[skewed_cols].skew().round(2))

    print("\nAfter transformation:")
    print(df_transformed[skewed_cols].skew().round(2))
    return df_transformed, skewed_cols

Log Transformation Analysis¶

Results¶

Log transformation had mixed effectiveness across features:

  • Insulin: Most improved — skewness reduced from 2.49 to -0.17, now close to normal distribution.

  • DiabetesPedigreeFunction: Meaningful improvement (1.99 → 1.17) but still moderately right-skewed.

  • Age: Partial improvement (1.22 → 0.68) but distribution shows multiple peaks, likely reflecting distinct age subgroups in the data.

  • Pregnancies: Over-corrected into slight left skew (1.02 → -0.21). Multiple peaks persist, suggesting discrete subgroups (e.g., 0, 1-2, 3+ pregnancies) that log transformation cannot smooth out.

Skewness Summary¶

Feature Before After
Pregnancies 1.02 -0.21
Insulin 2.49 -0.17
DiabetesPedigreeFunction 1.99 1.17
Age 1.22 0.68

Key Takeaway¶

Log transformation is effective for Insulin but limited for the other features. The multimodal distributions in Age and Pregnancies reflect genuine data subgroups rather than simple skewness — a different transformation is unlikely to resolve this. Since tree-based models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) are scale and distribution agnostic, residual skewness in these features is unlikely to harm model performance.

In [31]:
def add_features(df_transformed, df_original):
    # Use original scale values - clinically meaningful
    df_transformed['Glucose_Insulin_Ratio'] = (
    df_original['Glucose'] / (df_original['Insulin'] + 1)
    )

    df_transformed['BMI_Age'] = (
    df_original['BMI'] * df_original['Age']
    )

    df_transformed['High_Glucose'] = (
    df_original['Glucose'] > 140
    ).astype(int)

Feature Engineering¶

Logistic Regression and SVM are linear/kernel-based models — they benefit greatly from explicitly encoded relationships between features. However, diabetes risk often depends on combinations of features, not just individual values.

For example:

  • High glucose alone may not indicate diabetes if insulin is also appropriately high
  • High BMI is more dangerous in older patients than younger ones

Manually creating features that encode these combinations helps the models capture interactions they would otherwise miss or require many more iterations to approximate.

These features will be tested across all candidate models (Logistic Regression, KNN, SVM, SGD). The best 1-2 performers will then be selected for hyperparameter tuning.

feature scaling , we use StandardScaler, as it is common method to scale the data¶

In [35]:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, SGDClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV

models = {
    'Logistic Regression': LogisticRegression(random_state=42, max_iter=1000),
    'KNN':                 KNeighborsClassifier(),
    'SVM (RBF kernel)':    CalibratedClassifierCV(SVC(random_state=42), cv=5),
    'SGD Classifier':      SGDClassifier(loss='log_loss', random_state=42, max_iter=1000)
}

result = []

for name, model in models.items():
    pip = Pipeline([
        ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
        ('model', model)
    ])

    pip.fit(x_train_imputed_transformed, y_train)

    y_pred = pip.predict(x_test_imputed_transformed)
    y_prob = pip.predict_proba(x_test_imputed_transformed)[:, 1]

    result.append({
        "model": name,
        "accuracy_score": round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred), 2),
        "precision_score": round(precision_score(y_test, y_pred), 2),
        "recall_score": round(recall_score(y_test, y_pred), 2),
        
    })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(result)
results_df

1 KNN 0.69 0.55 0.58
2 SVM (RBF kernel) 0.74 0.62 0.60
3 SGD Classifier 0.66 0.51 0.46

Model Selection Analysis¶

Baseline Results (Default Parameters)¶

After training four candidate models on the same dataset, the following results were observed:

Model Accuracy Precision Recall
Logistic Regression 0.72 0.60 0.58
KNN 0.69 0.55 0.58
SVM (RBF Kernel) 0.74 0.62 0.60
SGD Classifier 0.66 0.51 0.46

Why Recall Is Our Primary Metric¶

In a medical classification problem, not all errors are equal.

  • A False Negative (predicting non-diabetic when the patient is diabetic) means a sick patient goes undiagnosed and untreated — a serious clinical risk.
  • A False Positive (predicting diabetic when the patient is not) leads to further testing — inconvenient but not harmful.

Therefore, we prioritize Recall on the diabetic class (class 1) over overall accuracy. A model that scores high accuracy by mostly predicting class 0 is not useful in healthcare.

Model Elimination¶

SGD Classifier — Eliminated

  • Recall : 0.46 — worst among all models.
  • This means SGD missed 54% of actual diabetic patients, making it clinically unreliable.
  • Its lower accuracy (0.66) and precision (0.51) further confirm it is not suitable.

KNN — Deprioritized

  • Recall : 0.58 — tied with Logistic Regression but lower accuracy (0.69) and lower precision (0.55).
  • Not eliminated, but SVM and Logistic Regression are stronger candidates.

Remaining Candidates¶

SVM (RBF Kernel) — Best overall: highest accuracy (0.74), precision (0.62), and recall (0.60).

Logistic Regression — Close second: slightly lower across all metrics but more interpretable and faster to tune.

These two will proceed to hyperparameter tuning.

ROC Curve Comparison¶

The ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve plots True Positive Rate (Recall) against False Positive Rate across all possible classification thresholds.

A perfect model scores AUC = 1.0. A random classifier scores 0.5 (the diagonal). The closer the curve hugs the top-left corner, the better the model's discriminative ability — independent of any threshold choice.

Model ROC-AUC
Logistic Regression 0.768
SVM (RBF Kernel) 0.755

Logistic Regression edges out SVM in overall discriminative ability. Both models perform significantly better than random chance (0.5 baseline). The curves track closely throughout, confirming neither model dominates clearly — threshold tuning will be the deciding factor.

Cross-Validation — Model Stability Check¶

A single train/test split can be misleading — the model might perform well or poorly simply due to how the data happened to be split. Cross-validation trains and evaluates the model across 5 different splits to check whether performance is consistent.

CV ROC-AUC Scores: [0.879, 0.843, 0.837, 0.852, 0.816] Mean ROC-AUC: 0.845 Std Deviation: 0.021

A standard deviation of 0.021 is very low — the model performs consistently across different data splits and is not overfitting to any one particular split.

Note: The CV mean (0.845) is higher than the test ROC-AUC (0.755). This is expected — cross-validation runs on training data only, which the model has seen during fitting. The test set represents truly unseen data, giving a more realistic performance estimate.

Threshold Tuning — Why This Matters Clinically¶

The Problem with Default Threshold (0.50)¶

Machine learning classifiers output a probability score between 0 and 1 for each patient. By default, sklearn labels a patient as diabetic only if that probability is ≥ 0.50. This treats false positives and false negatives as equally costly.

In diabetes screening, they are not equal:

Error Type What Happens Clinical Impact
False Negative (missed diabetic) Patient told they are healthy No treatment → serious long-term harm
False Positive (incorrect flag) Patient flagged for follow-up Additional testing → inconvenient, not harmful

At threshold 0.50, Logistic Regression misses 40% and SVM misses 44% of actual diabetic patients. In a real screening program, this is clinically unacceptable.

The Solution — Lower the Threshold¶

By lowering the threshold, we flag more patients as diabetic. This deliberately increases false positives in order to reduce the more dangerous false negatives. This is not a model fix — it is a conscious clinical decision about how to deploy the model responsibly.

Threshold Analysis — Both Models Evaluated¶

We evaluated both Logistic Regression and SVM across multiple thresholds to find the optimal operating point for each.

Logistic Regression¶

Threshold Recall (Diabetic) Precision (Diabetic) Accuracy
0.50 (default) 0.60 0.62 0.74
0.380 0.74 0.54 0.70
0.225 0.84 0.49 0.64

SVM (RBF Kernel)¶

Threshold Recall (Diabetic) Precision (Diabetic) Accuracy
0.50 (default) 0.56 0.65 0.74
0.278 0.72 0.49 0.648
0.234 0.80 0.47 0.61

Model Comparison at Optimal Thresholds¶

After finding the best threshold for each model, we compared them directly:

Metric LR (threshold 0.380) SVM (threshold 0.234)
Recall (Diabetic) 0.74 0.80
Precision (Diabetic) 0.54 0.47
F1 (Diabetic) 0.63 0.59
Accuracy 0.70 0.61
ROC-AUC 0.768 0.755

Final Decision — Logistic Regression at Threshold 0.380¶

Logistic Regression at threshold 0.380 is selected as the final model.

Why Logistic Regression Wins¶

This model is a first-line screening tool, not a diagnostic tool. The primary objective is to minimize missed diabetic cases — but precision cannot be ignored entirely. A model wrong on the majority of its positive predictions undermines clinical trust in the flagging system.

Given this context, the tradeoff favors Logistic Regression:

  • LR retains precision above 0.50 (0.54) — the model is still correct more often than not when flagging a patient as diabetic
  • SVM at 0.234 drops precision to 0.47 — meaning the majority of patients flagged as diabetic are actually healthy, which is clinically hard to justify
  • LR achieves better F1 (0.63 vs 0.59), higher accuracy (0.70 vs 0.61), and stronger ROC-AUC (0.768 vs 0.755)
  • LR recall of 0.74 means 37 out of 50 diabetic patients are correctly identified — a 14 percentage point improvement over the default threshold

SVM's higher recall (0.80) comes at the cost of tipping precision below 0.50, which is not a tradeoff worth making when LR already delivers strong recall with better performance across every other metric.

Important Limitation¶

Neither model should be used as a standalone diagnostic tool. All patients flagged as diabetic must be referred for confirmatory clinical testing — HbA1c measurement, fasting glucose test, or oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) — before any diagnosis is made.

This model's role is to prioritize who needs urgent evaluation, not to replace clinical judgment.

Healthcare Insights — What the Model Learned About Diabetes Risk¶

Feature importance was extracted from the tuned Logistic Regression model's coefficients. A positive coefficient means the feature increases predicted diabetes risk; a negative coefficient means it decreases it.

Feature Coefficient Direction
Age 1.707 ↑ Risk
BMI 1.543 ↑ Risk
Glucose 1.311 ↑ Risk
DiabetesPedigreeFunction 0.482 ↑ Risk
Pregnancies 0.418 ↑ Risk
BloodPressure -0.023 ↓ Risk (negligible)
SkinThickness -0.043 ↓ Risk (negligible)
Insulin -0.043 ↓ Risk (negligible)
High_Glucose -0.193 ↓ Risk (captured by Glucose)
Glucose_Insulin_Ratio -0.241 ↓ Risk (multicollinearity)
BMI_Age -1.587 ↓ Risk (multicollinearity)

Insight 1 — Age Is the Strongest Single Risk Factor (1.707)¶

Age has the highest coefficient in the model, meaning older patients carry significantly higher diabetes risk even after controlling for all other features.

This is clinically well established — insulin sensitivity decreases with age, and the pancreas gradually loses its ability to compensate. In this dataset, the Pima Indian women are aged 21–81, and age alone is a strong discriminator between diabetic and non-diabetic patients.

Clinical takeaway: Screening frequency should increase with patient age, particularly after 45.

Insight 2 — BMI and Glucose Are Nearly Equal in Importance (1.543, 1.311)¶

BMI and Glucose are closely weighted, together forming the core predictive signal in this model.

  • High BMI indicates excess adipose tissue, which causes insulin resistance — the body produces insulin but cells stop responding to it effectively.
  • High Glucose is the direct biochemical marker of that failure — blood sugar rises when insulin cannot move it into cells.

These two features appearing together at the top confirms that obesity-driven insulin resistance is the dominant mechanism in this dataset.

Clinical takeaway: BMI reduction through lifestyle intervention is one of the most evidence-backed methods for preventing Type 2 diabetes onset.

Insight 3 — Genetic Risk Is Real But Secondary (0.482)¶

DiabetesPedigreeFunction, which encodes hereditary diabetes likelihood based on family history, ranked 4th. It contributes meaningfully but is outweighed by modifiable factors like BMI and Glucose.

Clinical takeaway: Family history is a risk factor but not a sentence — patients with high DPF scores benefit most from early lifestyle interventions targeting BMI and glucose control.

Insight 4 — Pregnancies Contribute Modest Risk (0.418)¶

Higher number of pregnancies is associated with increased diabetes risk, likely reflecting gestational diabetes history. Each pregnancy can temporarily impair insulin sensitivity, and repeated episodes compound long-term risk.

Clinical takeaway: Women with multiple pregnancies, especially those with a history of gestational diabetes, should be prioritized for regular screening.

Insight 5 — BMI_Age Has a Large Negative Coefficient (-1.587)¶

BMI_Age was engineered as the product of BMI × Age to capture their combined effect. The large negative coefficient is a multicollinearity artifact — both BMI (1.543) and Age (1.707) already carry strong positive coefficients individually. When all three are present in the model, the interaction term absorbs conflicting weight to satisfy the regression equation, flipping its sign.

This does not mean high BMI combined with old age is protective — the opposite is clinically true. The coefficient reflects mathematical redistribution between correlated features, not a real-world relationship.

Do not interpret BMI_Age's coefficient as a clinical finding.

Insight 6 — Glucose_Insulin_Ratio Has a Negative Coefficient (-0.241)¶

A negative coefficient on Glucose_Insulin_Ratio means a higher ratio is associated with lower predicted diabetes probability in the model's learned weights. This is counterintuitive but reflects a multicollinearity effect — Glucose already carries a strong positive coefficient (1.311), and the ratio is partially redundant with it. The model redistributes weight across correlated features, which can flip the sign of engineered features.

The ratio still contributed to model performance during training, but its coefficient should not be interpreted in isolation as a clinical finding.

Insight 7 — SkinThickness, BloodPressure and Insulin Are Negligible¶

All three have near-zero coefficients (-0.023, -0.043, -0.043), meaning after accounting for BMI, Glucose, and Age, they add almost no predictive information.

SkinThickness was also the second most missing feature (29.56%), which likely reduced its signal quality despite KNN imputation. BloodPressure was the only feature with no clear boxplot separation between classes — consistent with its negligible coefficient here.

Clinical takeaway: These features may not be worth collecting in a streamlined screening workflow — Glucose, BMI, Age, and family history carry the majority of the predictive signal.

Summary — Top Risk Factors Ranked¶

Rank Feature Type
1 Age Non-modifiable
2 BMI Modifiable
3 Glucose Modifiable (diet, medication)
4 DiabetesPedigreeFunction Non-modifiable
5 Pregnancies Non-modifiable

A practical diabetes screening tool for this population could focus on just these five features and retain most of the model's predictive power.

Project Summary¶

Problem¶

Binary classification to predict diabetes onset in Pima Indian women using clinical measurements, with recall on the diabetic class as the primary metric.

Pipeline Overview¶

Stage Decision
Data Cleaning Replaced physiologically impossible zeros with NaN, dropped critical rows, imputed with KNN
Leakage Prevention Train/test split performed before KNN imputation and scaling
Feature Engineering Added High_Glucose, Glucose_Insulin_Ratio, BMI_Age
Log Transformation Applied to Insulin, DiabetesPedigreeFunction, Age, Pregnancies
Models Evaluated Logistic Regression, KNN, SVM (RBF), SGD Classifier
Tuning GridSearchCV with ROC-AUC scoring
Final Model Logistic Regression, C=100, threshold=0.380

Final Model Performance¶

Metric Default (0.50) Tuned (0.380)
Recall (Diabetic) 0.60 0.74
Precision (Diabetic) 0.62 0.54
F1 (Diabetic) 0.61 0.63
Accuracy 0.74 0.70
ROC-AUC 0.768 0.768

Key Findings¶

  • Age, BMI, and Glucose are the three dominant risk factors
  • BloodPressure and SkinThickness contribute negligible signal
  • Threshold tuning improved diabetic recall by 14 percentage points with precision remaining above 0.50
  • CV std of 0.021 confirms the model is stable and not overfitting

Limitations¶

  • Dataset is small (768 rows) and specific to Pima Indian women — generalization to other populations is not guaranteed
  • KNN imputation was required for 5 features, introducing some uncertainty in the training signal
  • This is a screening tool only — all positive predictions require confirmatory clinical testing before diagnosis

Every metric matches within noise once each model is evaluated at its own properly-tuned threshold. The engineered features are not contributing measurable predictive signal.

Decision: drop the engineered features. They add pipeline complexity (extra computation the deployed website would need to replicate exactly) and were already flagged as producing uninterpretable, sign-flipped coefficients from multicollinearity — with no offsetting benefit in recall, precision, accuracy, or ROC-AUC. The simpler feature set is used going forward, and this also serves as a reminder to always re-tune the decision threshold whenever the underlying feature set or model changes, rather than reusing one carried over from a previous configuration.

def find_best_threshold(model, x_test, y_test, target_recall=0.80):
    y_prob = model.predict_proba(x_test)[:, 1]
    precisions, recalls, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_test, y_prob)
    viable = [(t, p, r) for t, p, r in zip(thresholds, precisions[:-1], recalls[:-1]) if r >= target_recall]
    if not viable:
        return None, y_prob
    best_threshold, best_precision, best_recall = max(viable, key=lambda x: x[1])
    return (best_threshold, best_precision, best_recall), y_prob

def best_threshold(model, x_test, y_test, target_recall=0.80):
    result, _ = find_best_threshold(model, x_test, y_test, target_recall)
    print(f"best precision and recall for model: {result}")
    return result[0] if result is not None else None

for name, grid in [('Random Forest', rf_grid), ('Extra Trees', et_grid), ('Gradient Boosting', gb_grid)]:
    result, y_prob = find_best_threshold(grid.best_estimator_, x_test_no_eng, y_test)
    if result is None:
        print(f"{name}: no threshold reaches recall >= 0.80")
    else:
        t, p, r = result
        print(f"{name}: threshold={t:.3f}, precision={p:.3f}, recall={r:.3f}, ROC-AUC={round(roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob),3)}")

Random Forest: threshold=0.349, precision=0.524, recall=0.860, ROC-AUC=0.785
Extra Trees: threshold=0.498, precision=0.548, recall=0.800, ROC-AUC=0.785

Stage 2: Tree-Based Hyperparameter Tuning & Threshold Selection — Final Comparison¶

Note on CV vs. Test Gap¶

CV ROC-AUC during grid search (0.860–0.864) ran noticeably higher than test-set ROC-AUC (0.773–0.785) for all three tree ensembles — a gap not seen with Logistic Regression or SVM. This is likely GridSearchCV selecting the single best-scoring hyperparameter combination across many candidates, which can optimistically fit the specific CV folds used. Test-set numbers below are the ones used for the final decision, not the CV scores.

Full Model Comparison (all thresholds independently tuned for recall ≥ 0.80)¶

Model Threshold Recall Precision Accuracy ROC-AUC
Logistic Regression 0.380 0.74 0.54 0.70 0.768
Random Forest 0.349 0.86 0.524 0.683 0.785
Extra Trees 0.498 0.80 0.548 0.703 0.785
Gradient Boosting 0.322 0.80 0.541 0.697 0.773

Decision: Random Forest is the new leading candidate¶

Random Forest is the first model to beat Logistic Regression's recall by a meaningful margin (0.86 vs. 0.74) while still holding precision above the 0.50 floor that disqualified SVM earlier. It also ties Extra Trees for the best test ROC-AUC (0.785), ahead of both Logistic Regression (0.768) and Gradient Boosting (0.773).

Extra Trees and Gradient Boosting land essentially together (recall 0.80, similar precision/ROC-AUC to each other and close to Logistic Regression), but neither distinguishes itself from LR enough to justify the added model complexity over Random Forest's clearer recall improvement.

Random Forest (max_depth=6, min_samples_split=10, min_samples_leaf=1, n_estimators=100, threshold=0.349) is selected pending the final ROC curve and confusion matrix comparison across all models.

Final Model Comparison — Consistent Threshold Methodology (Target Recall ≥ 0.80)¶

All four models' thresholds were re-selected using their exact (unrounded) values from precision_recall_curve, applying the identical target-recall-≥-0.80 rule used originally to disqualify SVM — including, this time, Logistic Regression.

Model Threshold Precision Recall ROC-AUC TP FN FP TN
Logistic Regression 0.245 0.49 0.84 0.766 42 8 44 51
Random Forest 0.349 0.52 0.86 0.785 43 7 39 56
Extra Trees 0.498 0.55 0.80 0.785 40 10 33 62
Gradient Boosting 0.322 0.54 0.80 0.773 40 10 34 61

Correction to earlier methodology¶

Applying LR's threshold search with the same strict recall-≥-0.80 target used for the other models (rather than the looser target used in the original LR-vs-SVM comparison) reveals that Logistic Regression's precision falls to 0.49 — below the 0.50 floor that originally disqualified SVM. Under a consistent standard, Logistic Regression does not meet the same bar it was previously selected on. This does not invalidate the original LR-vs-SVM decision (SVM's recall/precision tradeoff was worse on both metrics at the time), but it means LR should not be treated as the baseline finalist going into the final model choice — Random Forest, Extra Trees, and Gradient Boosting are the three actual candidates that clear the precision floor at recall ≥ 0.80.

Random Forest vs. Extra Trees — the recall/precision trade¶

Random Forest catches 3 more true diabetic cases than Extra Trees (43 vs. 40, out of 50 in the test set), at the cost of 6 more false positives (39 vs. 33, out of 95 non-diabetic cases). Consistent with this project's stated priority — a missed diabetic patient (false negative) is more costly in a screening context than an unnecessary follow-up test (false positive) — this trade favors Random Forest: 6 additional follow-up tests is a low cost relative to catching 3 more actual diabetic cases that would otherwise go undiagnosed.

Final Decision¶

Random Forest (max_depth=6, min_samples_split=10, min_samples_leaf=1, n_estimators=100, threshold≈0.349) is selected as the final model: highest recall (0.86) and tied-best ROC-AUC (0.785) among all candidates that clear the minimum precision floor. Extra Trees remains a viable, more conservative alternative (precision 0.55, recall exactly at the 0.80 floor, 6 fewer false positives) if the ~41% false-positive rate of Random Forest proves too aggressive during real-world use on the deployed website — but given the explicit priority of minimizing missed diagnoses over minimizing follow-up tests, Random Forest is the better fit for a screening tool.

ROC Curve Comparison — All Models¶

The ROC curve overlay confirms the pattern seen in the metrics table. Random Forest and Extra Trees (AUC = 0.79 each) trace curves that sit above Logistic Regression and Gradient Boosting (AUC = 0.77 each) across most of the false-positive-rate range, particularly in the low-to-mid FPR region (0.0–0.4) that matters most for a screening tool — this is the region where you're deciding how aggressively to flag patients while keeping false alarms low.

Extra Trees (green) shows the steepest early rise, reaching close to 0.6 true positive rate before 0.2 false positive rate — the best "bang for the FPR" of any model in this range. Random Forest (orange) tracks close behind, with a few local dips (e.g. its bump around FPR 0.2–0.3) but converges to the same overall AUC and pulls ahead near the top of the curve. Logistic Regression (blue) and Gradient Boosting (red) largely overlap each other through the middle of the curve, consistently trailing the two tree ensembles.

All four curves sit well clear of the diagonal random-classifier reference line across the full range, confirming each model captures real predictive signal well beyond chance. The visual result is consistent with the numeric comparison: Random Forest and Extra Trees are the two strongest candidates, and Logistic Regression does not distinguish itself from Gradient Boosting despite being the simpler model.

class DiabetesRiskModel:
    def __init__(self, pipeline, threshold):
        self.pipeline = pipeline      # the real fitted RF pipeline — full sklearn API available via this
        self.threshold = threshold

    def predict_risk(self, X):
        """Your custom threshold-aware prediction — what the API calls."""
        prob = self.pipeline.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
        return (prob >= self.threshold).astype(int)

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        """Pass-through, in case the API wants raw probabilities too."""
        return self.pipeline.predict_proba(X)

    def model(self):
        """Return the underlying pipeline."""
        return self.pipeline

    @property
    def feature_importances_(self):
        """Direct access to the underlying RandomForestClassifier's importances."""
        return self.pipeline.named_steps['model'].feature_importances_

Final Model Packaging for Deployment¶

The selected Random Forest pipeline (max_depth=6, min_samples_split=10, min_samples_leaf=1, n_estimators=100) is wrapped in a DiabetesRiskModel class that bundles the fitted pipeline together with its tuned decision threshold (≈0.349, selected for recall ≥ 0.80). This ensures any code calling the model — the API, a notebook, a teammate — automatically uses the correct threshold rather than sklearn's default 0.5, which was shown earlier in this notebook to produce meaningfully different (and less clinically appropriate) results.

The wrapper exposes:

  • predict_risk(X) — the primary prediction method, returns 0/1 using the tuned threshold
  • predict_proba(X) — raw class probabilities, for showing a risk percentage
  • feature_importances_ — direct access to the trained Random Forest's feature importances, for explaining predictions
  • .pipeline — the underlying fitted sklearn pipeline, for any other need (raw .predict() at 0.5, .get_params(), individual trees via .estimators_, etc.)

The object is serialized with joblib (preferred over raw pickle for sklearn models due to more efficient handling of the numpy arrays inside fitted estimators) and loaded once at API startup rather than per-request, to avoid repeated disk I/O.
